questions.stem: Which is an example of a portability requirement?

options.A: The system shall respond in under 2 seconds
options.B: The system shall run on Windows 10, Ubuntu 22.04, and macOS 14 without modification
options.C: Mean time to failure shall exceed 5,000 hours
options.D: The system shall encrypt data using AES-256

questions.explanation: Portability requirements specify how easily the system can be moved to new environments.

questions.stem: User requirements should avoid:
questions.explanation: User requirements must be readable by non-technical customers.

questions.stem: The cost amplification of late requirements errors occurs because fixing them requires:

options.B: Redesigning architecture, rewriting code, redoing tests, and potentially retraining users
options.C: Only adding a new test case

questions.explanation: Late fixes ripple through architecture, code, tests, and training.

questions.stem: The Appendices section of an SRD contains:

options.A: Detailed supporting information like hardware specs, database schemas, and external interface descriptions

questions.explanation: Appendices hold supporting material that would clutter the main document.

questions.stem: Natural language is the most commonly used notation because:

options.B: It is accessible to both technical and non-technical stakeholders
options.D: It is the most precise notation

questions.explanation: Accessibility is the main advantage of natural language.

questions.stem: The acronym VCCV stands for:
questions.explanation: VCCV is the FSEN 106 mnemonic for the four validation checks (plus Realism).

questions.stem: Which validation technique creates a test plan that can be used directly when testing the final system?
questions.explanation: Test cases generated during validation are reused during system testing.

questions.stem: Requirements management ensures that changes are:

options.B: Tracked, assessed, and incorporated in a controlled way

questions.explanation: Management does not prevent change; it controls it.

questions.stem: Requirements validation is the process of:

options.B: Checking that requirements in the SRD define the system the customer actually wants
options.D: Writing test cases for the code

questions.explanation: Validation confirms the SRD matches customer intent.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a reliability requirement?

options.A: The system shall respond in under 2 seconds
options.B: Mean time to failure shall exceed 5,000 hours; downtime shall not exceed 4 hours per month
options.C: All patient data shall be encrypted at rest
options.D: The system shall run on macOS 14

questions.explanation: Reliability requirements cover failure rates and recovery time.

questions.stem: Requirements engineering processes vary enormously between:

options.B: Different organisations and types of applications

questions.explanation: An aerospace system needs a very different RE process than an agile web app.

questions.stem: Consistency check asks:

options.B: 'Can all requirements be satisfied simultaneously? No two requirements should contradict each other.'

questions.explanation: Consistency means requirements do not conflict.

questions.stem: The intended audience for system requirements is:
questions.explanation: System requirements are detailed technical specifications for the development team.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a standard section of an IEEE 830 SRD?
questions.explanation: Marketing is not part of the IEEE 830 SRD structure.

questions.stem: Text highlighting in requirements (bold, italic) is used to:

options.B: Pick out key terms, actors, and system names

questions.explanation: Highlighting draws attention to critical elements within requirement text.

questions.stem: Validation may reveal missing requirements that require:
questions.explanation: The iterative nature means validation can trigger new elicitation.

questions.stem: Requirements engineering is one of the most critical phases because:

options.B: Mistakes made here are the most costly to correct later

questions.explanation: Requirements errors propagate downstream and amplify in cost.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a guideline for writing natural language requirements?

options.C: Avoid computer jargon in user requirements
options.D: Use as many ambiguous words as possible

questions.explanation: Ambiguity should be avoided, not embraced.

questions.stem: Finding a requirements error after delivery may cost:

options.A: The same as fixing it during requirements
options.B: Up to 100 times more than fixing it during requirements
options.C: Less than fixing it during requirements

questions.explanation: The cost amplification factor is up to 100x.

questions.stem: A requirement that cannot be tested is:

options.B: Worthless — requirements that cannot be tested are worthless

questions.explanation: Untestable requirements cannot be validated.

questions.stem: Closed interviews use:

options.A: Free discussion to explore topics in depth
options.B: Pre-defined questions for systematic information gathering

questions.explanation: Closed interviews follow a structured question set.

questions.stem: Ethnography is particularly effective for discovering:

options.B: Implicit requirements related to existing work practices that stakeholders take for granted

questions.explanation: Tacit work practices are visible to observers but invisible to interviewers.

questions.stem: SRD stands for:
questions.explanation: SRD = Software Requirements Document, also called SRS (Software Requirements Specification).

questions.stem: Graphical notations add value when:

options.B: Visual clarity adds value, especially for interaction and behavioural requirements

questions.explanation: Diagrams help stakeholders visualise complex interactions.

questions.stem: RE processes are:

options.B: Varied — different types of systems need different processes

questions.explanation: Process choice depends on system type, risk, and organisational context.

questions.stem: Each requirement is assigned a unique identifier so it can be:

options.A: Cross-referenced with other requirements, design components, test cases, and code modules

questions.explanation: Unique IDs enable traceability assessments.

questions.stem: The System Evolution section of an SRD anticipates:

options.B: Future changes and planned evolutionary modifications

questions.explanation: It documents fundamental assumptions and anticipated future requirements.

questions.stem: Errors in requirements documents are:

options.A: The cheapest type of software defect
options.B: The most expensive type of software defect
options.C: Easier to fix than code errors

questions.explanation: Requirements errors found after delivery can cost 100x more.

questions.stem: Prototyping as a validation technique is particularly effective for:

options.A: Discovering missing requirements and validating usability requirements

questions.explanation: Prototypes make abstract requirements concrete and testable.

questions.stem: Which notation is most appropriate for safety-critical avionics software?
questions.explanation: Safety-critical systems need completely unambiguous formal notation.

questions.stem: Workshops and focus groups are useful for:

options.A: Resolving conflicting viewpoints across stakeholder groups and reaching consensus quickly

questions.explanation: A skilled facilitator manages group discussion to reach consensus.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a constraint, not a service?

options.A: The system shall generate monthly invoices
options.B: The system shall use no more than 512 MB of server storage
options.C: The system shall allow users to log in
options.D: The system shall send email confirmations

questions.explanation: Storage usage is a constraint on the system, not a service it provides.

questions.stem: System managers use the SRD to:

options.B: Plan bids, estimate cost and timeline, and plan the development process

questions.explanation: Managers use the SRD for bidding and project planning.

questions.stem: Traceability policies define:

options.A: Relationships between each requirement and between requirements and system design

questions.explanation: Traceability links enable impact analysis.

questions.stem: Conflicting requirements cause:

options.B: Inconsistencies that may only surface during integration testing

questions.explanation: Conflicts may remain hidden until integration, when they cause failures.

questions.stem: Questionnaires and surveys are useful for:

options.A: Gathering statistical data about user priorities across large populations

questions.explanation: Surveys scale to large stakeholder populations but lack depth.

questions.stem: Structured natural language uses:

options.B: Predefined templates with fixed fields to improve consistency

questions.explanation: Templates reduce flexibility but improve consistency across the document.

questions.stem: Which is a primary output of the requirements engineering process?

options.B: A description of system services and constraints

questions.explanation: RE outputs are descriptions of services plus constraints.

questions.stem: Scenarios can be used to develop:
questions.explanation: Scenarios often evolve into formal use cases.

questions.stem: Each requirement should have a unique identifier to enable:
questions.explanation: Unique IDs (e.g., FR-001, NFR-012) allow cross-referencing.

questions.stem: Requirements prioritisation is part of:
questions.explanation: Prioritisation and conflict resolution happen during analysis.

questions.stem: Ambiguous requirements typically lead to:
questions.explanation: Ambiguity means each developer may implement a different interpretation.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a reason requirements change?
questions.explanation: Grammar fixes are edits, not requirement changes.

questions.stem: Functional requirements describe:

options.B: What the system should do — services, reactions to inputs, and behaviours

questions.explanation: Functional requirements declare services the system must provide and behaviours it must exhibit.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a space requirement?

options.A: Mean time to failure shall exceed 5,000 hours
options.B: The system footprint on the server shall not exceed 512 MB of storage excluding the database
options.C: The system shall run on Windows 10, Ubuntu 22.04, and macOS 14
options.D: The system shall process 1,000 records per minute

questions.explanation: Space requirements constrain memory or disk usage.

questions.stem: Validation asks 'Are we building the right system?' This is different from verification, which asks:
questions.explanation: Validation = right system; verification = system built right.

questions.stem: Mathematical specifications (Z, VDM, finite state machines) are used for:

options.B: Safety-critical systems where ambiguity is unacceptable

questions.explanation: Formal methods are completely unambiguous but hard to validate with customers.

questions.stem: Which stakeholder group signs off on the SRD as part of the contract?
questions.explanation: Customers verify and formally sign off on the SRD.

questions.stem: User requirements are typically written for:

options.B: Customers and end-users in natural language

questions.explanation: User requirements target non-technical stakeholders in natural language with diagrams.

questions.stem: Which is NOT an elicitation technique listed in FSEN 106?
questions.explanation: Code review is a quality activity, not an elicitation technique.

questions.stem: Which notation is most appropriate for a high-level user requirement?
questions.explanation: User requirements need accessibility over precision.

questions.stem: A banking system must implement interest calculations according to specific regulatory formulas. This is:
questions.explanation: The regulatory interest formula is a domain-specific computation.

questions.stem: System requirements are written for:

options.B: Developers and architects as detailed technical specifications

questions.explanation: System requirements specify precise, testable detail for the development team.

questions.stem: Verification asks:
questions.explanation: Verification checks the implementation against the specification.

questions.stem: A requirement that 'the system shall send automated reminder notifications 24 hours before appointments' is:
questions.explanation: It describes a specific service the system provides.

questions.stem: Requirements serve a dual function as a basis for:

options.A: A contract bid AND as the basis for the contract itself

questions.explanation: The dual function: requirements inform the contract bid and become the basis of the contract.

questions.stem: Requirements engineering bridges the gap between:

options.B: What the customer needs and what the development team builds

questions.explanation: RE translates customer needs into implementable specifications.

questions.stem: System customers use the SRD to:

options.B: Specify requirements; read and verify the document matches their needs; sign off as part of the contract
options.D: Track progress and manage scope changes

questions.explanation: Customers verify and sign off on the SRD.

questions.stem: Structured natural language is preferred when:

options.B: A standard format is required across the organisation

questions.explanation: Templates improve consistency in organisational settings.

questions.stem: Reviews can be:

options.B: Formal (structured inspection with roles) or informal (walkthrough)

questions.explanation: Both styles are valid; formality depends on project risk.

questions.stem: Which activity produces an organised requirement set with logical structure?
questions.explanation: Classification groups raw requirements into coherent clusters.

questions.stem: Realism check asks:

options.B: 'Can the requirements be implemented within budget, on schedule, and using available technology?'

questions.explanation: Realism verifies feasibility.

questions.stem: Natural language notation is best used for:

options.A: Safety-critical systems where ambiguity is unacceptable
options.B: User requirements and high-level system requirements where accessibility matters more than precision

questions.explanation: Natural language is accessible but can be ambiguous.

questions.stem: Completeness check asks:

options.B: 'Is anything the customer expects missing from the specification?'

questions.explanation: Completeness means all expected functions and constraints are present.

questions.stem: A requirement may range from:

options.A: A single test case to a test suite
options.B: A high-level abstract statement to a detailed mathematical specification
options.C: A user story to a deployment plan
options.D: A use case to a sequence diagram

questions.explanation: Requirements span high-level abstractions for stakeholders down to precise mathematical specs.

questions.stem: The first stage of the elicitation and analysis process is:
questions.explanation: Discovery involves interacting with stakeholders to uncover needs.

questions.stem: Post-requirements traceability links requirements to:

options.B: The design components and tests that implement them

questions.explanation: Post-requirements traceability goes forward to implementation.

questions.stem: The User Requirements section of an SRD is written using:

options.A: Natural language and diagrams, accessible to non-technical stakeholders

questions.explanation: User requirements must be readable by customers.

questions.stem: The tension in requirements specification is that:

options.A: More precise requirements are easier to read
options.B: More precise requirements are harder to read; simpler ones are more ambiguous

questions.explanation: Specification must balance precision with readability.

questions.stem: Draft requirements documentation is suitable for:
questions.explanation: The draft is iteratively refined.

questions.stem: Trade-offs in requirements are resolved during:
questions.explanation: Analysis negotiates and resolves trade-offs.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a maintainability requirement?

options.A: Any licensed developer familiar with Python shall be able to understand and modify a module within 2 hours
options.B: The system shall respond in under 2 seconds
options.C: All data shall be encrypted using AES-256
options.D: Mean time to failure shall exceed 5,000 hours

questions.explanation: Maintainability requirements cover ease of modification and extension.

questions.stem: A useful strategy for catching ambiguity is to ask:

options.B: 'How would I test this?' If the test is unclear, the requirement is ambiguous

questions.explanation: Testability is a key signal of clarity.

questions.stem: Stakeholders often describe:

options.B: What they currently do, rather than what they need

questions.explanation: Users tend to describe the status quo; analysts must infer needs.

questions.stem: IEEE Std 830 defines:

options.B: The recommended standard structure for Software Requirements Specifications

questions.explanation: IEEE 830 standardises the structure of SRS documents.

questions.stem: Product requirements specify that the delivered product must:

options.B: Behave in a particular way regarding execution, reliability, or memory usage
options.D: Be developed using a specific methodology

questions.explanation: Product requirements cover execution speed, reliability, and memory/disk usage.

questions.stem: Over-specified requirements can:

options.B: Waste development effort on unnecessary features

questions.explanation: Over-specification spends effort on features the customer did not really need.

questions.stem: The Preface section of an SRD defines:
questions.explanation: The Preface covers version history, reasons for changes, scope, and intended audience.

questions.stem: Specialist requirements management tools mentioned in FSEN 106 include:

options.A: IBM DOORS, Jira, and Azure DevOps

questions.explanation: These tools store requirements, manage change requests, and track traceability.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a quality attribute typically covered by NFRs?
questions.explanation: Brand awareness is a marketing concern, not a system quality attribute.

questions.stem: Non-functional requirements are best described as:

options.B: Constraints on services or functions offered by the system

questions.explanation: NFRs constrain properties and qualities rather than specific behaviours.

questions.stem: Requirements engineering is best defined as the process of:

options.A: Writing source code for a software system
options.B: Establishing the services a customer requires from a system and the constraints under which it operates
options.C: Designing the user interface of a software system
options.D: Testing a software system against user expectations

questions.explanation: RE establishes services required plus constraints under which the system operates and is developed.

questions.stem: An example of an invalid requirement is one that:

options.A: Does not actually deliver value to the user

questions.explanation: Invalid requirements do not serve real customer needs.

questions.stem: Requirements reviews are most cost-effective when:
questions.explanation: Early reviews catch errors before they propagate.

questions.stem: Verifiability check asks:

options.A: 'Can a test be written that will objectively confirm the requirement has been met?'

questions.explanation: Verifiability means each requirement has an objective test.

questions.stem: The text states that non-functional requirements are often:
questions.explanation: Failure to meet an NFR can render the entire system unusable even if all FRs are met.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a component of requirements management planning?
questions.explanation: Marketing is not part of requirements management.

questions.stem: Workshops are faster than:
questions.explanation: One workshop can replace many sequential interviews.

questions.stem: The System Architecture section of an SRD provides:

options.B: A high-level overview of anticipated system structure

questions.explanation: It describes distribution of functions across modules and major components.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-functional requirement?

options.A: The system shall allow users to reset their password
options.B: The system shall load in under 2 seconds
options.C: The system shall send an email confirmation
options.D: The system shall generate monthly invoices

questions.explanation: Response time is a performance non-functional requirement.

questions.stem: To check consistency, you can use:

options.A: A requirements matrix to identify conflicts

questions.explanation: Matrices reveal contradictions between requirements.

questions.stem: To check completeness, you can:

options.A: Ask stakeholders 'Is anything missing?' and use checklists based on the problem domain

questions.explanation: Domain checklists and stakeholder dialogue surface gaps.

questions.stem: The improved version 'The system shall support a minimum of 500 concurrent users without degradation' is better because:
questions.explanation: Measurable criteria make the requirement testable.

questions.stem: Skilled requirements engineers:

options.B: Choose and combine techniques based on system type, stakeholder availability, and nature of requirements

questions.explanation: No single technique fits all situations.

questions.stem: Which keyword is used for mandatory requirements?
questions.explanation: SHALL indicates a mandatory requirement.

questions.stem: Every requirement should correspond to:
questions.explanation: Test-case generation during validation creates a usable test plan.

questions.stem: A baseline is:

options.B: A formally agreed version of the requirements at a specific point in time

questions.explanation: Baselines are formally agreed reference points.

questions.stem: Functional requirements must be:

options.C: Written only in formal mathematical notation

questions.explanation: All required services must be defined and no two should conflict.

questions.stem: Requirements engineering is described as:
questions.explanation: New requirements emerge during development and the process repeats.

questions.stem: Domain language barriers cause problems because:

options.A: Developers may misunderstand technical terminology used in the application domain
options.D: Domain language is forbidden in requirements

questions.explanation: Domain-specific terms can be misinterpreted by non-domain developers.

questions.stem: The disadvantage of mathematical specifications is that they are:
questions.explanation: Customers typically cannot read formal notation.

questions.stem: Domain requirements are derived from:

options.A: The application domain of the system

questions.explanation: Domain requirements reflect characteristics and rules of the specific application domain.

questions.stem: Which technique is BEST for gathering data from thousands of users?
questions.explanation: Surveys scale to large populations efficiently.

questions.stem: Which technique is BEST when stakeholders cannot articulate abstract needs?
questions.explanation: Concrete prototypes reveal latent requirements.

questions.stem: Project management uses the SRD to:

options.A: Track progress, manage scope changes, and assess impact of proposed changes

questions.explanation: PM uses the SRD as the baseline against which scope changes are assessed.

questions.stem: Which requirement identifier scheme is recommended?
questions.explanation: Unique IDs enable traceability and change management.

questions.stem: Requirements reviews involve:

options.A: Manual analysis by a team of reviewers, including both customer and contractor staff

questions.explanation: Reviews are most effective when customers and developers participate together.

questions.stem: In practice, the four RE activities are:

options.B: Interleaved and iterative rather than sequential

questions.explanation: RE is a spiral process where activities are revisited.

questions.stem: Incomplete stakeholder availability leads to:
questions.explanation: Missing stakeholders mean missing perspectives.

questions.stem: The output of requirements discovery is:

options.B: An initial draft of unorganised stakeholder needs

questions.explanation: Discovery produces raw, unstructured requirements.

questions.stem: 'The system shall authenticate users via SHA-256 hashed passwords stored in PostgreSQL using bcrypt with salt factor 12' is an example of:
questions.explanation: It specifies HOW the system behaves including protocols and storage details.

questions.stem: Requirements elicitation includes:

options.B: Understanding stakeholder goals, needs, and constraints

questions.explanation: Elicitation covers stakeholder identification and goal/need/constraint discovery.

questions.stem: The example 'The system shall support a large number of users' is problematic because:

options.B: 'Large' is ambiguous — does it mean 10, 10,000, or 1 million?

questions.explanation: Ambiguous quantifiers must be replaced with measurable criteria.

questions.stem: Requirements management is the process of:

options.B: Managing changing requirements during the RE process and throughout the system development lifecycle

questions.explanation: Management does not prevent change; it controls it.

questions.stem: To check verifiability, you should:

options.A: Draft a test case for each requirement

questions.explanation: If a test cannot be written, the requirement is ambiguous or unmeasurable.

questions.stem: Step 2 of the change management process is:
questions.explanation: Traceability information is used to assess impact and estimate cost.

questions.stem: Requirements elicitation is also called:
questions.explanation: Elicitation involves discovering requirements by working with stakeholders.

questions.stem: Functional requirements depend on:

options.A: The type of software being developed

questions.explanation: FRs depend on software type, user type, and overall system context.

questions.stem: Which technique is BEST for resolving conflicts across many stakeholder groups?
questions.explanation: Workshops bring conflicting parties together for negotiation.

questions.stem: The change management process has how many steps?
questions.explanation: Steps: Problem Analysis, Change Analysis & Costing, Acceptance/Rejection, Implementation.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a security requirement?

options.A: The system shall respond in under 2 seconds
options.B: All patient data shall be encrypted at rest using AES-256; all connections shall use TLS 1.3 or higher
options.C: The system shall run on Windows 10
options.D: Medical staff shall be trained in 4 hours

questions.explanation: Security requirements protect data and systems from unauthorised access.

questions.stem: A railway signalling system must comply with safety interlocking rules. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Safety interlocking rules are specific to the railway signalling domain.

questions.stem: An ambiguous requirement typically:

options.B: Has more than one possible interpretation

questions.explanation: Ambiguity means multiple valid interpretations exist.

questions.stem: Which validation technique is most cost-effective when done early?
questions.explanation: Reviews are cheap and surface different classes of problems when done early.

questions.stem: The output of RE feeds directly into:
questions.explanation: RE outputs are inputs to design and validation activities.

questions.stem: Requirements volatility means that requirements:

options.B: Change during analysis as the business environment evolves

questions.explanation: Volatility is a normal feature of RE.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a stakeholder group listed in FSEN 106 as using the SRD?
questions.explanation: Marketing is not listed as a stakeholder group for the SRD.

questions.stem: Requirements validation asks:
questions.explanation: Validation checks that requirements match what customers actually want.

questions.stem: Which is the BEST example of a measurable non-functional requirement?

options.B: The system shall respond to user input within 200 milliseconds under normal load
options.D: The system shall be easy to use

questions.explanation: Measurable NFRs include specific thresholds that can be tested.

questions.stem: When a change is implemented, the system is:

options.B: Retested in all affected areas; version control records the change history

questions.explanation: Affected areas are retested to ensure no regressions.

questions.stem: Step 1 of the change management process is:
questions.explanation: First, the problem or improvement is formally specified.

questions.stem: A hospital system correctly lists all appointments (functional) but is too slow to be usable. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: The function works but the performance quality attribute fails.

questions.stem: Some requirements may be deferred to:
questions.explanation: Prioritisation may push lower-priority requirements to later releases.

questions.stem: Design description languages are:

options.B: Rarely used for requirements; more appropriate for system design and algorithm specification

questions.explanation: DDLs resemble programming languages and are too implementation-focused for requirements.

questions.stem: The four generic activities common to all RE processes are:
questions.explanation: These are the four core RE activities.

questions.stem: Different stakeholders have:
questions.explanation: Conflict between stakeholders is normal and must be negotiated.

questions.stem: Ethnography reveals:

options.B: Social and political constraints on the system

questions.explanation: Embedded observation surfaces social and political realities.

questions.stem: Which statement about NFRs is TRUE?

options.A: NFRs apply only to single features
options.B: Even if every FR is perfectly implemented, the system can still fail if NFRs are not met
options.C: NFRs are less critical than FRs

questions.explanation: NFR failure can render the whole system unusable regardless of FR success.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a consequence of poorly engineered requirements?
questions.explanation: Poor requirements never improve code quality; they degrade project outcomes.

questions.stem: Open interviews allow:

options.B: Free discussion to explore topics in depth

questions.explanation: Open interviews are exploratory and unconstrained.

questions.stem: UML graphical notations for requirements include:

options.A: Use-case diagrams, sequence diagrams, activity diagrams, state charts

questions.explanation: UML provides multiple graphical notations for system requirements.

questions.stem: The Glossary section of an SRD:

options.A: Lists all technical and domain terms alphabetically

questions.explanation: The Glossary defines terms so readers do not need specialised knowledge.

questions.stem: Changes to baselined requirements must go through:
questions.explanation: Baselines are stable; changes require formal approval.

questions.stem: Unstated assumptions are dangerous because:

options.B: Stakeholders assume they are obvious and will be included automatically, but they may not be
options.D: They have no impact on the system

questions.explanation: Implicit assumptions must be surfaced and made explicit.

questions.stem: Poor requirements are a leading cause of:
questions.explanation: Industry studies repeatedly identify poor requirements as the top cause of project failure.

questions.stem: The System Models section of an SRD typically includes:

options.A: Data flow diagrams, ER diagrams, UML use case and sequence diagrams

questions.explanation: System Models provide graphical representations of structure and behaviour.

questions.stem: Which validation technique is particularly effective for usability requirements?
questions.explanation: Usability is best validated by interacting with a working model.

questions.stem: The iterative nature of RE is:
questions.explanation: Iteration reflects the reality that understanding develops over time.

questions.stem: The SRD should describe:

options.B: What the system should do, not how it achieves its goals

questions.explanation: The SRD is a requirements document, not a design document.

questions.stem: To check realism, you should:

options.A: Validate with developers and architects; cost unrealistic delivery

questions.explanation: Developers and architects know what is technically feasible.

questions.stem: An example of an untestable requirement is:

options.A: The system shall respond within 200 ms
options.C: The system shall support 500 concurrent users
options.D: The system shall encrypt data using AES-256

questions.explanation: 'User-friendly' is subjective and cannot be objectively tested.

questions.stem: Use cases are a UML technique that:

options.A: Identify actors and describe their interactions with the system

questions.explanation: Use case diagrams show scope; use case descriptions detail interactions.

questions.stem: Tool support for requirements management is essential because:

options.A: Manual tracking is sufficient for large systems
options.B: Large systems involve large volumes of information that manual processes cannot handle

questions.explanation: Scale demands tool support.

questions.stem: During requirements analysis, conflicting requirements from different stakeholders must be:
questions.explanation: Conflicts require structured negotiation.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a usability requirement?

options.A: The system shall respond in under 2 seconds
options.B: Medical staff shall be able to perform all primary functions after 4 hours of training
options.C: The system shall run on Windows 10
options.D: Mean time to failure shall exceed 5,000 hours

questions.explanation: Usability requirements define ease of use for the intended user class.

questions.stem: A limitation of interviews is that they may:

options.A: Miss tacit knowledge that stakeholders do not realise they hold

questions.explanation: Tacit knowledge is hard to articulate; ethnography surfaces it.

questions.stem: A requirement 'The system shall allow users to log in with their student ID' is an example of:
questions.explanation: It focuses on WHAT at a high level without implementation detail.

questions.stem: The SRD is the official statement of:

options.A: What the system developers should implement
options.B: How the system achieves its goals

questions.explanation: The SRD specifies WHAT, not HOW.

questions.stem: Functional requirements may also explicitly state:

options.A: What the system should NOT do to prevent misuse

questions.explanation: FRs may state prohibitions to prevent unsafe or unwanted behaviour.

questions.stem: The SRD serves as a communication bridge between:

options.B: All stakeholders involved in a software project

questions.explanation: The SRD is read by every stakeholder group, each using it differently.

questions.stem: Who uses the SRD to develop validation test plans?
questions.explanation: Testers derive validation test plans directly from SRD requirements.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a performance requirement?

options.A: The system shall run on Windows 10
options.B: The MHC-PMS shall process up to 1,000 patient records per minute under normal load
options.C: All patient data shall be encrypted at rest using AES-256
options.D: Medical staff shall be able to perform all primary functions after 4 hours of training

questions.explanation: Performance requirements specify response time or throughput.

questions.stem: A System Requirements Specification section in an IEEE 830 SRD contains:

options.A: Both functional and non-functional requirements in precise, testable form

questions.explanation: This section is the technical core of the SRD.

questions.stem: In UML, an actor is:

options.A: A person or external system that interacts with the system

questions.explanation: Actors are external entities that interact with the system under development.

questions.stem: A standard format for every requirement in the document:

options.B: Makes the document easier to read and reduces missing information
options.D: Is only needed for non-functional requirements

questions.explanation: Consistency aids readability and completeness.

questions.stem: Validation checks for which FIVE properties?
questions.explanation: FSEN 106 lists these five validation checks.

questions.stem: Automated analysis tools (e.g., IBM DOORS) are useful for:

options.B: Large documents with hundreds or thousands of requirements where manual review is impractical

questions.explanation: Tools scale where manual review cannot.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about requirements is FALSE?

options.A: Requirements describe what the system should do
options.B: Requirements describe constraints under which the system operates
options.C: Requirements are always static once written
options.D: Requirements can range from abstract to detailed mathematical specifications

questions.explanation: Requirements evolve throughout development; they are not static.

questions.stem: The people who pay for the system are not always the same people who use it. This leads to:

options.B: Conflicting priorities between sponsors and users

questions.explanation: Divided stakeholders create evolving priorities.

questions.stem: Which elicitation technique is mentioned in FSEN 106 as a 'formal UML technique'?
questions.explanation: Use cases are formalised within the UML standard.

questions.stem: System test engineers use the SRD to:

options.B: Develop validation test plans and test cases directly from requirements

questions.explanation: Testers derive test plans and test cases from the SRD.

questions.stem: An MHC-PMS requirement that 'a user shall be able to search the appointments lists for all clinics' is:
questions.explanation: It specifies a service the system must provide.

questions.stem: Organisational and political factors may:

options.B: Influence what requirements are stated or suppressed

questions.explanation: Politics can cause stakeholders to suppress or advance requirements for personal agendas.

questions.stem: Step 4 of the change management process is:
questions.explanation: If accepted, the SRD and design are modified and the system is retested.

questions.stem: The dual role of requirements means they must be written to be:

options.A: Open to interpretation AND precisely defined

questions.explanation: Requirements must serve both stakeholders (need interpretation) and developers (need precision).

questions.stem: Domain requirements may be expressed in:

options.B: The technical language of the application domain

questions.explanation: Domain requirements use domain-specific terminology that non-experts may not understand.

questions.stem: Which activity produces an agreed, prioritised requirements set with documented conflict resolutions?
questions.explanation: Negotiation produces prioritised, agreed requirements.

questions.stem: Which IEEE standard governs SRS structure?
questions.explanation: IEEE Std 830 is the recommended practice for SRS.

questions.stem: Ethnography is:

options.B: An observational technique where an analyst embeds in the working environment

questions.explanation: Ethnography observes actual work practices as they happen.

questions.stem: Scenarios and stories help stakeholders:

options.B: Concretise vague needs by thinking through specific examples

questions.explanation: Concrete scenarios reveal missing requirements and edge cases.

questions.stem: System maintenance engineers use the SRD to:

options.A: Understand system structure and design rationale for future modifications

questions.explanation: Maintainers need to understand structure and rationale for safe modification.

questions.stem: Changes during development require:

options.B: Management to track, assess, and incorporate them

questions.explanation: Change management is a core RE activity.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes 'requirements engineering'?

options.A: A one-time activity at project start
options.B: An ongoing spiral process throughout development

questions.explanation: RE is iterative and revisits earlier activities as understanding develops.

questions.stem: Requirements specification is the process of:

options.B: Writing down user and system requirements in a formal requirements document

questions.explanation: Specification is the act of formally documenting requirements.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a characteristic of functional requirements?
questions.explanation: Execution speed is a non-functional (performance) requirement.

questions.stem: Which activity involves working with stakeholders to discover requirements?
questions.explanation: Elicitation is the discovery activity.

questions.stem: A requirement is testable if:

options.A: You can write a test that confirms whether the requirement is met

questions.explanation: Testability is a core requirement quality.

questions.stem: Requirements classification groups requirements based on:

options.B: Related functionality, subsystems, or requirement types

questions.explanation: Classification imposes logical structure on raw requirements.

questions.stem: Missing requirements result in:

options.B: Features the customer expected but never received

questions.explanation: Missing requirements mean expected features never get built.

questions.stem: SRS stands for:
questions.explanation: SRS = Software Requirements Specification, an alternative name for the SRD.

questions.stem: Requirements management does NOT try to:

options.D: Incorporate approved changes in a controlled way

questions.explanation: Change is inevitable; management controls rather than prevents it.

questions.stem: An SRD differs from a design document because the SRD:

options.B: Specifies WHAT the system should do

questions.explanation: The SRD specifies WHAT; design documents specify HOW.

questions.stem: Following IEEE 830 ensures the SRD has:
questions.explanation: IEEE 830 standardises structure to ensure no essential components are omitted.

questions.stem: The phrase 'requirements engineering bridges the gap between' emphasises that RE:

options.B: Translates customer needs into implementable specifications

questions.explanation: RE is the translation layer between customer needs and developer deliverables.

questions.stem: Requirements must be written clearly enough to be understandable to:

options.B: Both customers (who validate) and developers (who implement)

questions.explanation: The document serves dual audiences.

questions.stem: Effective requirements management requires:

options.A: Establishing policies and processes before development begins

questions.explanation: A management plan must be in place before changes start arriving.

questions.stem: Step 3 of the change management process is:

options.A: Change acceptance or rejection (with documented rationale)

questions.explanation: Stakeholders decide to accept, defer, or reject; rationale is documented.

questions.stem: The Index section of an SRD provides:

options.A: Navigation aids including alphabetical and requirements indexes

questions.explanation: The Index helps readers find specific content quickly.

questions.stem: Validity check asks:

options.B: 'Will satisfying this requirement actually deliver value to the user?'

questions.explanation: Validity is about whether the requirement delivers real customer value.

questions.stem: New legislation or updated regulations may require:

options.A: System modifications after requirements have been agreed

questions.explanation: Regulatory changes force post-baseline requirement changes.

questions.stem: Organisational requirements arise from:
questions.explanation: Organisational requirements come from internal policies including process standards and delivery constraints.

questions.stem: Automated analysis tools can check for:
questions.explanation: Tools detect common defects automatically.

questions.stem: The Introduction section of an SRD describes:

options.A: The need for the system, target users, constraints, assumptions, dependencies

questions.explanation: The Introduction covers system functions overview, target users, and project context.

questions.stem: Pre-requirements traceability links requirements to:
questions.explanation: Pre-requirements traceability goes backward to stakeholder needs.

questions.stem: Use case diagrams give:

options.B: An overview of system scope and actors

questions.explanation: Diagrams show scope; descriptions detail interactions.

questions.stem: External requirements arise from:

options.B: Factors external to the system such as laws and regulations

questions.explanation: External requirements include interoperability, legislative compliance, and ethical requirements.

questions.stem: Prototyping may reveal that:

options.A: Stakeholders imagined the system differently from how developers understood the requirements

questions.explanation: Concrete prototypes expose mismatched mental models.

questions.stem: Requirements validation is described as one of the highest-ROI activities because:

options.B: Time and effort invested in thorough validation pays dividends throughout the rest of the project
options.C: It eliminates the need for testing

questions.explanation: Validation prevents expensive late-stage rework.

questions.stem: Mistakes made during the requirements phase are described as:

options.B: The most costly to correct later in the lifecycle

questions.explanation: Requirements errors propagate through design, code, and tests, making them the most expensive to fix late.

questions.stem: Test-case generation as a validation technique serves to:

options.B: Reveal unmeasurable, ambiguous, or incomplete requirements
options.C: Eliminate the need for testing later

questions.explanation: If you cannot write a test, the requirement is flawed.

questions.stem: Mixing WHAT and HOW in the SRD is:

options.B: A common mistake that leads to premature design commitments

questions.explanation: Mixing concerns limits implementation options and causes rework.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes RE as a 'spiral activity'?

options.A: RE happens once at project start
options.B: RE cycles back as new requirements emerge
options.C: RE only happens at project end

questions.explanation: Spiral implies iterative revisiting of activities.

questions.stem: Including rationale for each requirement helps:
questions.explanation: Rationale explains why a requirement exists, helping with future trade-offs.

questions.stem: A requirement that the system use a specific coding standard is an:
questions.explanation: Coding standards arise from organisational policies.

questions.stem: Which keyword is used for desirable but optional requirements?
questions.explanation: SHOULD indicates a desirable but not mandatory requirement.

questions.stem: At key project milestones, the requirements set is formally:
questions.explanation: Baselining provides stability against scope creep.

questions.stem: Use case descriptions provide:

options.B: Detailed interaction steps, preconditions, and postconditions

questions.explanation: Descriptions are the textual counterpart to diagrams.

questions.stem: A limitation of questionnaires is that they:

options.A: Cannot follow up on interesting answers without additional contact

questions.explanation: Surveys are one-shot; deeper follow-up requires another method.

questions.stem: Stakeholders may not be able to articulate requirements until they see a:
questions.explanation: Prototypes make abstract needs concrete.

questions.stem: If domain requirements are not satisfied, the system may be:

options.A: Unworkable even if technically correct from a software perspective

questions.explanation: Domain requirements reflect domain rules; ignoring them makes the system unfit for purpose.

questions.stem: A large safety-critical aerospace system requires:

options.A: The same RE process as a small web app
options.B: A very different RE process than an agile web application startup

questions.explanation: RE processes scale with system risk and complexity.

questions.stem: Change analysis and costing uses:

options.A: Traceability information to identify all affected requirements, design, code, and tests

questions.explanation: Traceability is what makes impact analysis possible.

questions.stem: Interviews are best suited for:

options.A: Understanding high-level goals, priorities, and known requirements
options.D: Resolving conflicts across many stakeholder groups simultaneously

questions.explanation: Interviews reveal what stakeholders consciously know.

questions.stem: Requirements analysis involves:

options.B: Checking collected requirements for consistency, completeness, and conflicts

questions.explanation: Analysis identifies conflicts, sets priorities, and resolves trade-offs.

questions.stem: An MHC-PMS requirement that 'each staff member shall be uniquely identified by an 8-digit employee number' is:
questions.explanation: It specifies behaviour the system must implement.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a category of non-functional requirement mentioned in FSEN 106?
questions.explanation: The three categories are Product, Organisational, and External.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a typical problem caused by poor requirements?

options.B: System fails to meet user expectations

questions.explanation: Poor requirements have no positive effect on compilation speed.

questions.stem: System requirements specify:

options.B: Exactly HOW the system behaves including error handling, data formats, and protocols

questions.explanation: System requirements specify detailed behaviour including error handling and protocols.

questions.stem: Research consistently shows that requirements errors are:

options.A: The cheapest type of software defect
options.B: The most expensive type of software defect
options.C: Easier to fix than coding errors
options.D: Found only during user acceptance testing

questions.explanation: A requirements defect found after deployment can cost 100x more to fix.

questions.stem: Words like 'will' or 'may' in requirements are:
questions.explanation: Use SHALL for mandatory and SHOULD for desirable; avoid 'will' and 'may'.

questions.stem: Requirements elicitation and analysis is challenging because:

options.A: Stakeholders always know precisely what they want
options.B: Stakeholders often do not know precisely what they want
options.D: Domain language is always clear to developers

questions.explanation: Stakeholders frequently cannot articulate their needs until they see a prototype.

questions.stem: The output of the requirements engineering process is:

options.B: Descriptions of system services and constraints

questions.explanation: RE produces descriptions of services plus constraints under which the system operates.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the four core RE activities?
questions.explanation: Compilation is a code activity, not a requirements activity.

questions.stem: The change management process decides:

options.A: Whether a proposed change should be accepted, deferred, or rejected based on cost-benefit analysis

questions.explanation: Each change is evaluated for cost vs. benefit.

questions.stem: Baseline management provides:
questions.explanation: Formal change control prevents uncontrolled expansion of scope.

questions.stem: Which technique is BEST for discovering implicit work practices?
questions.explanation: Observation surfaces tacit knowledge.

questions.stem: Software projects without properly engineered requirements risk:

options.A: Delivering products that fail to meet user expectations

questions.explanation: Poor requirements lead to all three failure modes.

questions.stem: Prioritisation and negotiation output:

options.B: Agreed, prioritised requirements with conflict resolutions documented

questions.explanation: Negotiation produces agreed, prioritised, documented requirements.

questions.stem: Non-functional requirements often apply to:

options.B: The system as a whole rather than individual features

questions.explanation: NFRs are typically system-wide properties like reliability or performance.

questions.stem: A requirement that the system comply with GDPR is an:
questions.explanation: GDPR is an external legal regulation.

questions.stem: Domain requirements can introduce:
questions.explanation: Domain requirements may add FRs, constrain existing ones, or define domain-specific computations.

questions.stem: The SRD should include:

options.C: Both user requirements and system requirements

questions.explanation: SRD serves both customers (user reqs) and developers (system reqs).

questions.stem: Requirements documentation produces:

options.B: A draft requirements document suitable for review, validation, and baseline agreement

questions.explanation: The draft is iteratively refined.

questions.stem: User requirements focus on:

options.A: HOW the system behaves including error handling
options.B: WHAT the system should do at a high level, avoiding implementation details

questions.explanation: User requirements focus on the WHAT, not the HOW.

questions.stem: User requirements may include:

options.A: Abstract descriptions of system services and operational constraints

questions.explanation: User requirements are high-level, abstract, and accessible to customers.

questions.stem: Prototyping is particularly effective when:

options.A: Stakeholders find it difficult to articulate requirements in the abstract

questions.explanation: Seeing a prototype surfaces requirements stakeholders did not know they had.

questions.stem: Which type of requirement specifies how the system must respond to particular inputs?
questions.explanation: Functional requirements define system reactions to inputs including error conditions.

questions.stem: An IEEE 830 SRD's Index section primarily provides:

options.B: Navigation aids including alphabetical and requirements indexes

questions.explanation: The Index helps readers find specific content quickly.

questions.stem: Which elicitation technique is BEST for surfacing social and political constraints on the system?
questions.explanation: Embedded observation surfaces social and political realities.

questions.stem: When a stakeholder says 'the system should be fast', the requirements engineer should:

options.B: Replace 'fast' with a measurable criterion like 'respond within 200ms'
options.D: Convert it to a domain requirement

questions.explanation: Vague quantifiers must be replaced with measurable criteria for testability.
